events.description: Afghan communist coup, followed by uprisings against the new government
Soviet invasion/intervention; major Soviet units introduced in late December 1979
Soviet Union withdrew last combat forces from Afghanistan

A Soviet battalion raided a Mujahideen ammunition storage area deep in the mountains, whose location an Afghan informer had revealed. The Afghan guide became lost, and the battalion commander returned to the area where earlier rockets had landed. He reasoned the rockets were pre-registered on the route, and the guide became reoriented and the mission continued.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; chemical/toxin attacks on Mujahideen were reported as early as six months before.
US government received reports of 47 separate toxic agent attacks against Mujahideen with a death toll of more than 3000 (unsubstantiated).
A Soviet battalion raid to destroy a Mujahideen ammunition storage area, located via an Afghan informer; the battalion commander reoriented a lost Afghan guide by returning to a rocket impact area.
Afghan Communist Party coup, after which the COIN effort began.
Soviet combat forces introduced into Afghanistan, framed as an 'intervention' in an ongoing COIN effort.
By mid-1980 the Soviets acquired additional missions: eliminating insurgent centers, separating insurgents from the population, interdicting outside aid and sanctuary.
Masood abandoned defense of the Panjsher Valley and organized Mujahideen groups to attack strategic approaches across the Hindu Kush.
Afghan communist coup, followed by uprisings against the new government.
Soviets introduced major units into Afghanistan in late December, beginning the war.
Soviets installed Babrak Karmal as new Afghan communist leader.
Soviet Union withdrew its last combat forces from Afghanistan after nine years.
Masood gave up defending the Panjsher Valley and organized Mujahideen groups to attack approaches across the Hindu Kush.

key_claims: Mujahideen lacked unified leadership and strategic planning, but this disunity hindered Soviet infiltration of their leadership.
Mujahideen groups affiliated with political organizations in Pakistan or Iran mainly to obtain weapons, supplies and intelligence.
Mujahideen had sanctuaries in Pakistan and Iran and significant outside material support.
Ahmad Shah Masood abandoned static defense of the Panjsher and trained groups to attack strategic approaches across the Hindu Kush.
The Soviet Union's Limited Contingent was constrained in size, leaving areas vulnerable when forces were concentrated elsewhere.
Combat experience gained by Soviet officers in Afghanistan will have a significant impact on the quality of training in the Soviet Army for the next several years.
Soviet doctrine may not change greatly, but tactical, combat support and combat service support skills should be enhanced.
Some Soviet tactical commanders showed quick thinking, such as a battalion commander who deduced that rockets were pre-registered on the route to a Mujahideen ammunition storage area.
The Mujahideen's weapons progressed from small arms and machine guns up to 12.7mm to RPGs, mortars, recoilless rifles and free rockets by mid-war.
Soviet decontamination equipment is mounted on trucks and thus presents a soft target.
Reports of toxic agents in rockets, bombs, sprays and landmines could not be substantiated.
